topics.title: Design tokens — how do you structure them so theming doesn't collapse?
topics.html:
Tier 1 primitive blue-500, gray-100, space-4, font-size-14 ← raw values, no meaning Tier 2 semantic color.text.primary, color.bg.danger, space.inline.sm Tier 3 component button.primary.bg → color.bg.brand Components consume tier 2/3 ONLY. Nobody imports blue-500 directly.
  • The whole value is in tier 2: a dark theme is a different mapping of semantic → primitive, not a second set of components.
  • One source of truth — tokens exported from Figma (Style Dictionary / Tokens Studio) into CSS variables and a TS theme object. Two sources means permanent drift.
  • Naming by role, never by appearance: color.text.danger, not color.text.red — otherwise your red token turns orange and the name lies forever.
  • CSS custom properties beat JS theme objects for runtime theming: switching a theme is a class on <html>, with zero re-render.
💬 Say it like this

I use three levels. Primitives are raw values with no meaning. Semantic tokens give them a role — text primary, background danger. Component tokens connect the parts of a component to semantic tokens. Components use only the semantic level, so adding a dark theme means changing one mapping file instead of every component. And I name tokens by role, not by colour, because when "red" later becomes orange the name is wrong forever.

How do you keep Figma and code in sync?
Tokens live in Figma variables, exported to JSON, transformed into CSS variables and TS types in CI. A drift check in the pipeline fails the build if the generated file differs from what's committed.

topics.title: How do you version and ship a shared UI kit that ten teams depend on?
topics.html:
• Monorepo: pnpm workspaces + Turborepo. Changesets for versioning: every PR that changes behaviour adds a changeset, releases and changelogs are generated.
  • Semver seriously: a renamed prop is a major. Ship a deprecation first — accept both props, warn in dev, remove one major later.
  • Codemods for breaking changes (jscodeshift). "Upgrade and here's the script" gets adoption; "upgrade and fix 300 call sites" gets ignored.
  • Public API surface: the exports map controls what's importable — internals stay internal. Tree-shakeable ESM build, sideEffects: false.
  • Docs are the product: Storybook with usage, props, do/don't, and a11y notes. A component nobody can find gets rebuilt locally for the fourth time.
  • Quality gates: visual regression (Chromatic/Playwright screenshots), axe checks in CI, bundle-size budget per component.
  • Adoption metric: percentage of app screens using kit components vs local one-offs. That's the number to report upward.
💬 Say it like this

Technically it is a monorepo with Changesets, strict semver and a tree-shakeable build. But the hard part is not the tooling, it is adoption. So a breaking change always comes with a deprecation period and a codemod script, and the Storybook docs have to be good enough that using the kit is faster than writing your own button. I also measure adoption — how many screens still use their own local components — because that number shows if the design system really works.

A team needs a variant your component doesn't support.
First ask whether it's a genuine new semantic case or a one-off. If genuine, add a variant to the API. If one-off, give them composition — slots, asChild, style overrides through tokens — rather than a fifteenth boolean prop.

topics.title: "Design a data table / a chat / a feed." How do you structure the answer?
topics.html:
1. Clarify scope (1 min). How much data, how fresh, who uses it, mobile or desktop, offline? Ask two or three questions — this alone separates senior from mid.
  2. API contract. Shape of the response, pagination style (cursor beats offset for feeds), what the server owns vs the client.
  3. Rendering strategy. Server-rendered shell? Streaming? Client-only behind auth?
  4. State model. Server state in React Query, UI state local, shareable state (filters, sort, page) in URL params so a link reproduces the view.
  5. Performance. Virtualization above a few hundred rows, memoized row components, deferred filter input, images sized to avoid CLS.
  6. Edge cases. Empty, loading, error, partial failure, permissions, very long strings, RTL, slow network.
  7. Accessibility. Semantic table markup or ARIA grid, keyboard navigation, focus management, announced updates.
  8. Rollout. Feature flag, metrics to watch, how you'd roll back.
// Filters in the URL — shareable, back-button friendly, survives reload
const [params, setParams] = useSearchParams();
const sort = params.get("sort") ?? "date";
const { data } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ["orders", { sort, page }],       // the key IS the state
  queryFn: ({ signal }) => api.orders({ sort, page }, signal),
  placeholderData: keepPreviousData,          // no flicker between pages
});
💬 Say it like this

I would start with a few questions, because the answer is completely different for ten rows and for a hundred thousand. Then I go layer by layer: the API contract and pagination, where the data lives — server data in React Query, filters in the URL so the view can be shared — then rendering and performance, and at the end the states people forget: empty, error, permissions and keyboard support. I would also say what I would measure after release.

topics.title: Accessibility — what do you actually do, beyond "add aria-labels"?
topics.html:
• Semantics first. A real <button> gives you focus, Enter/Space, and screen-reader role for free. Most ARIA exists to repair markup that shouldn't have been a div.
  • Keyboard: everything clickable is reachable and operable; visible focus ring; logical tab order; no keyboard traps.
  • Modals: focus moves in on open, is trapped inside, returns to the trigger on close; Escape closes; background is inert/aria-hidden.
  • Async updates: aria-live="polite" for toasts and results counts, role="alert" for errors — otherwise a screen reader user never learns the save failed.
  • Forms: every input has a real label; errors are tied via aria-describedby; never colour alone to signal state.
  • Testing: axe in CI, tab through the feature yourself, and Testing Library's getByRole — if the role query can't find your element, neither can a screen reader.
💬 Say it like this

My first rule is to use the right element — a real button instead of a clickable div — because that gives keyboard support and the correct role for free. Then I check three things in every feature: can I finish the task with the keyboard only, does focus work correctly in dialogs, and are async results announced. I also use getByRole in tests, because if the test cannot find the element by role and name, a screen reader cannot either.
